comments.text:
This sounds great, but I’ve got two big 'what-ifs' from a payor perspective:
First, the gaming risk. If a COIN agent can see the exact rules, it’ll eventually just learn how to pass the minimum requirements for a 'Yes' without actually giving us the whole clinical picture.

Second is the versioning. Getting every system to talk to each other is one thing, but keeping them on the same version of the rules at the same time? That’s a massive lift. Without that, I think we might run into more integration headaches.

If you and the community can pull this off though, this would be amazing, and I believe it's needed.

comments.text:
Fair point on the tools.

On the gaming side, my concern is FWA (Fraud, Waste, and Abuse). Working in the public sector, we're under a massive microscope, and that accountability falls on us if the system is drained by bad actors. We want the patient at the center, which means protecting the resources they rely on. If the rules are a 100% transparent 'cheat sheet' for fraud, it’s the patients who lose out in the long run.
The question now is: how do we solve for this? How do we balance open clinical logic with the necessary 'guardrails' to protect the program? 🤔

comments.text: For Medicare and Medicaid plans, payers are already publishing PA criteria in their provider portals, adding transparency but shifting the burden to providers navigating complex, payer-specific rules. While some discretion exists in documenting clinical necessity, payers are increasingly applying structured, evidence-based criteria that limit subjectivity. With advances in AI, it will be interesting to see how health plans are motivated to expose AI agent-ready APIs or MCP servers to streamline PA — reducing administrative burden on both sides. That said, HIPAA compliance, algorithmic bias, and fragmented AI governance across federal and state regulators remain real barriers to meaningful adoption.

comments.text:
fair point. I’m not suggesting we hide the 'how-to' for best-value care, that should definitely be out in the open for legitimate clinicians.
Thinking through it, the shift really needs to be from hiding the rules to verifying the facts. If we open up the logic like you’re suggesting, then 'Proof of Care' has to be the focus. Maybe the move is to lean into the provenance resource or even digital sigs at the resource level.
If we can create a solid verification layer where we can cryptographically trust that the data is tied to a real encounter, then the 'open rules' become much less of an FWA risk. It gives us(payors) the security we need for program integrity without making the honest providers jump through more manual hoops.
Does the SMART or HL7 roadmap have a clear path for standardizing that 'Proof of Care' layer yet?

comments.text:
Anna McCollister This was a great thought exercise and actually led me to build a Proof of Concept using Agentic AI to solve exactly this.
In the public sector, fraud and abuse aren't theoretical problems, they are a massive accountability we have to manage. My approach moves the security from hiding the rules to verifying the facts. By applying a cryptographic fingerprint to the clinical data straight from the EHR, we can keep the rules 100% open and transparent. If a bad actor tries to game those open rules with fake data, the seal breaks and the rules never even run.
It gives the honest clinician a fast approval while putting up a mathematical wall against fraud. We stop protecting the secret and start verifying the truth. That is the better way forward.

author.headline: Senior Project Manager | Healthcare Interoperability | FHIR | AI | Digital Health Innovation

comments.text:
It sounds very similar to the challenges we face in Israel. While we have a centralized national health basket, each HMO  operates with its own internal 'black box' of clinical validation logic, especially for complex oncology protocols.
​The real breakthrough won't just be a digital pipe for requests, but making the HMOs' coverage rules computable. By leveraging FHIR’s Clinical Reasoning resources (like PlanDefinition and Library) combined with CQL, we could shift from a reactive 'wait and see' process to real-time transparency.
​Imagine an oncologist receiving a CDS Hook notification during the ordering process, confirming that the chemotherapy protocol meets the HMO’s specific criteria based on the patient’s latest lab results. That’s the level of transparency we need to reduce the administrative burden and, more importantly, the time-to-treatment for our patients.
